Keeps apart from a2e08 and a6e04: the student is trained on the teacher's answers, nothing is routed; no apprentice. The concert: the brief's school-leavers' concert sits in June or July, so the night keeps the season's October timeline and the concert is an all-ages show by a band whose fans are mostly still at school, which is why under-18 requests came in October. Timeline: the large model with its rules prompt answered every chat until Friday 25 September; its saved answers to the last 8,000 enquiries (about two months at about 120 a day: 8,000 / 120 = 66.7 days) trained the student; the check on 200 random older enquiries the student had not trained on was run on Thursday 24 September; the student went live on Saturday 26 September; in 6 days, about 720 enquiries, 720 x 11 / 8,000 = 0.99 under-18 expected, and the one that came was a phone call to Haukur on the day desk on Tuesday 29 September; tonight is Friday 2 October 2026: the concert ended at 21:30, 5 under-18 chats came 22:00 to 23:00, the student refused the one at 22:41 and booked four into Saturday 3 October; Ilvana reads tomorrow's list every night at 23:50, which is what alerted her. Every rate is a count from a stated set: 187 of 200 (93.5%), 200 x 11 / 8,000 = 0.275, 2,000 x 11 / 8,000 = 2.75, teacher 40 of 40 and student 9 of 40 on the must-refuse set, $0.02 / $0.001 = 20 times, 2 s / 0.4 s = 5 times. The under-18 rule is the parlour's own; no law is cited. Under-18 customers are described in general words only; the four booking notes quoted are short, name no one, and one is the brief's. title: The Student Who Copies

post.author: u/night_needle_ilvana
post.title: I'm the night artist at a tattoo parlour. At 23:50 I read tomorrow's list: four bookings for sixteen-year-olds, made by our booking assistant.

blocks.text: I'm Ilvana, the night artist at Esquith Street Tattoo. After we close at 20:00 I finish long pieces and draw stencils, the paper outlines, for tomorrow's customers. Our own rule is nobody under 18.

People book through a chat on our website. A booking assistant answers: a program that chats with them, then puts the booking on tomorrow's list. Under it sits a language model, a program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text.

Until last week it ran on a large model, big and capable. Before every chat it read a long rules prompt: standing orders with our prices, our hours, and the under-18 rule. Each chat cost about $0.02 and took about 2 seconds a reply.

Ms Sciarra, the owner, wanted it cheaper and quicker. She kept the large model's saved answers to our last 8,000 enquiries, about two months of chats. Then she trained a small model on them. In steps: it read an enquiry, guessed a reply, and its learned numbers were nudged toward the large model's answer.
It's a student copying a teacher's homework, so the large model is called the teacher and the small one the student.

Copying a big model into a small one this way is called distillation. The student reads no long prompt; the rules were meant to come through in the answers it copied. It costs $0.001 a chat and replies in 0.4 seconds.
Most of the 8,000 asked about availability, prices, aftercare or designs; those are our kinds of enquiry. Only 11 were from under-18s, and the teacher refused all 11.

Before switching, she checked the student. She drew 200 older enquiries it hadn't trained on, at random, like names from a hat, and compared its answers with the teacher's. They matched on 187 of 200, 93.5%. That share is called agreement. None of the 200 was from an under-18. At 11 in 8,000 you'd expect 200 × 11 ÷ 8,000 = 0.275 of one.

The student went live on Saturday 26 September. We get about 120 enquiries a day, so about 720 in 6 days, and 720 × 11 ÷ 8,000 is about one under-18. That one rang on Tuesday, and Haukur on the day desk said no.

Tonight, Friday 2 October, the arena down the road had an all-ages concert by a band whose fans are mostly still at school. It ended at 21:30. Our booking form asks no age. The rule lived only in the teacher's prompt.
At 23:50 I read tomorrow's list, as I do every night. The assistant copies a line from each chat into the booking's note. Each line below shows when it booked, tomorrow's slot, and that note.

22:06  10:00  I'm 16, it's my first one
22:19  11:30  16, after the concert
22:34  13:00  I'm 16
22:52  14:30  16, small one on the wrist
Four bookings for sixteen-year-olds, made by a model whose teacher refused every one.

Then I read tonight's chats. Five under-18 requests came between 22:00 and 23:00. The student refused one, at 22:41, and booked the other four. I've cancelled the four, and Ms Sciarra will message each at 09:00.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at Esquith Street is haunted. Your student has no idea what 18 means. It never read the rules prompt; it only learned to answer the way the teacher answered in the examples it was shown. Amazon's guide to its model service uses the same names: a larger teacher, a smaller, faster student. Two questions. Of the 8,000 answers it learned from, how many showed the teacher saying no to an under-18? And of the 200 in Ms Sciarra's check, how many?

comments.author: u/good_enough_faolan
comments.text: Calm down. 93.5% agreement is a pass; four bad bookings in a week is noise. No model matches another all the time, and you cancelled them anyway. Don't let anyone talk your owner into a must-refuse set, a list of requests made up specially that the student must always turn down. That's days of work for one odd night. If you want more comfort, train it longer on the same answers so it agrees more, or check 2,000 random enquiries instead of 200. Either way, keep the saving.

replies.author: u/night_needle_ilvana
replies.text: Ms Sciarra liked the part about keeping the saving.

comments.author: u/day_desk_haukur
comments.text: I took Tuesday's call. A young lad rang to book, said he was 16, and I said no and told him why. I never thought to mention it; the assistant had always said no too. If it can't be trusted, put the large model back on every chat until the small one is fixed. We paid $0.02 a chat before and we managed.

replies.author: u/night_needle_ilvana
replies.text: Ms Sciarra says that's 20 times the cost and 5 times as slow, for a fix with no end date.

reply.prompt: The four bookings are cancelled, and Ms Sciarra wants to keep the student. What should Esquith Street change before the next busy night? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Train the small model longer on the same 8,000 answers until it agrees more.
options.part2: On Saturday 3 October Ms Sciarra trained the student for longer on the same 8,000 answers. In the sim its agreement on the 200 rose from 187 to 191 of 200 (95.5%), and she was pleased. Then Haukur and I wrote 40 under-18 requests on purpose, the kind a sixteen-year-old might send, and ran them. The teacher refused 40 of 40. The student refused 10 of 40, one more than before. Every pass over the same answers showed it the same 11 refusals; there was nothing new to learn from. It had got better at the kinds it already did well. On Friday 9 October another under-18 request came by chat, and it booked it.
options.senior: More training on the same examples sharpens what the examples already teach. The refusal lived in 11 of 8,000, about 1 in 727, too few to learn a rule from, and more passes don't add any. A higher agreement on a random sample mostly measures the common kinds getting better.

options.text: Check its agreement with the large model on 2,000 random enquiries instead.
options.verdict: A bigger hat, the same few
options.part2: On Saturday 3 October Ms Sciarra drew 2,000 random older enquiries. The student agreed on 1,870 of 2,000, 93.5% again. You'd expect 2,000 × 11 ÷ 8,000 = 2.75 under-18s in a draw that size, and it held 3. The teacher refused all 3. The student refused 1 and booked 2. Two wrong answers out of 2,000 barely move the average, and nobody looked at them one by one. She kept the student. In the sim it still refuses only 9 of the 40 under-18 requests we later wrote on purpose, and the booking form still asks no age.
options.senior: Ten times the sample gives ten times the expected rare cases, 2.75 instead of 0.275, which is still almost none. A rare kind that the model gets wrong every time can sit inside a 93.5% average without moving it. Size the check by the rare kind, not by the total.

options.text: Score it per kind of enquiry, with a must-refuse set it must pass in full.
options.part2: On Saturday 3 October we scored the check of 200 one kind at a time: availability 89 of 92, prices 47 of 49, aftercare 31 of 34, designs 20 of 25, under-18 none in the sample at all. Then Haukur and I wrote 160 under-18 requests in the words people really use. 40 became the must-refuse set, kept apart. The student refused 9 of 40: stop. Ms Sciarra had the teacher answer the other 120, added them to the 8,000, and retrained the student on Sunday 4 October. On Monday 5 October the new student refused 40 of 40 requests it had never seen, and still agreed on 187 of 200. It went back live on Tuesday 6 October at $0.001 a chat. We also added an age question to the booking form, so the rule lives in two places now. Designs, at 20 of 25, are next on her list.
options.senior: A small task-specific model is measured per kind of request, never on one average. Write a set of the cases that must never go wrong, keep it apart from training, and require all of it to pass. If the student fails, give it more examples of that kind, answered by the teacher, and retrain. And keep a hard rule in the system too, not only in what a model learned.

options.text: Send every enquiry back to the large model until the small one is fixed.
options.part2: From Saturday 3 October every chat went back to the teacher with its long rules prompt. In the sim it refuses 40 of 40, and nothing under 18 got booked. But each chat cost $0.02 again, 20 times the student, and each reply took 2 seconds, 5 times as long. At 120 enquiries a day that is $2.40 a day instead of $0.12. And nothing was fixed: the student sat unused with the same gap, nobody wrote down what it would have to pass to come back, and three weeks later Ms Sciarra was asking again whether 93.5% was good enough.
options.senior: Falling back to the larger model is a fair way to stop the harm the same night, and sometimes it is the right long-term choice. But it pays 20 times the cost and 5 times the wait, and it skips the lesson: without a per-kind score and a must-pass set, there is no test that says when the student is ready.

sim.title: Score the student at Esquith Street
sim.lede: You're Ilvana at 21:30 on Friday 2 October, before tonight's chats. No real model runs here: every score is a given count. Given: the student trained on the teacher's saved answers to 8,000 enquiries: availability 3,600, prices 2,000, aftercare 1,400, designs 989, under-18 11, all 11 refused by the teacher. The check before switching drew 200 random older enquiries: availability 92 (the student agreed on 89), prices 49 (47), aftercare 34 (31), designs 25 (20), under-18 0, so 187 of 200. A 2,000 check: 905 (875), 497 (478), 352 (322), 243 (194), under-18 3 (refused 1), so 1,870 of 2,000. Trained longer: 191 of 200 and 1,910 of 2,000. The must-refuse set: 40 under-18 requests written on purpose; the teacher refuses 40, the student 9, or 10 trained longer, or 40 once 120 more written requests, with the teacher's refusals, are added to training. Teacher $0.02 and 2 seconds a chat; student $0.001 and 0.4 seconds. Tonight: 5 under-18 requests from 22:00 to 23:00; the student booked 4 and refused 1. Expected under-18s are the sample size × 11 ÷ 8,000.
sim.tryThis: Try this: as it is, agreement is 187 of 200 (93.5%) and 0.275 under-18s are expected in the sample, with none found. Play tonight: 4 of 5 booked. Switch to 2,000 random: 2.75 expected, 3 found, and still 93.5%. Score per kind: the must-refuse set stops it at 9 of 40. Switch the model to the teacher: 40 of 40 at $0.02 and 2 seconds a chat. Add the 120 written requests: the student passes 40 of 40 at $0.001. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Esquith Street was haunted. The parlour trained a small student model on a large teacher model's answers, and the under-18 rule reached the student only through 11 refusals in 8,000 examples, too few to learn. The check before switching was one average over 200 random enquiries, where 0.275 under-18s were expected and none appeared, so the one kind that had to be right was never tested.

steps.title: What distillation did, step by step.
steps.text: First, the teacher, the large model with its long rules prompt, answered real enquiries; the parlour kept those answers. Second, each enquiry and the teacher's answer became one training example, 8,000 in all. Third, the student, a small model with no rules prompt, read each enquiry, guessed a reply, and had its learned numbers nudged toward the teacher's answer, over many passes. Fourth, it was checked against the teacher on a sample and switched on. What can go wrong: the student learns only what the examples show. The rule itself was never in them, only 11 answers that happened to follow it.

steps.title: Why 11 in 8,000 is too few.
steps.text: Training nudges the student toward what its examples have in common. Availability questions made up 3,600 of the 8,000, so the student saw thousands of them. Under-18 requests made up 11, about 1 in 727, and each looked different, so there was no clear pattern to learn. On 40 under-18 requests written on purpose, the teacher refused 40 and the student 9. Training longer on the same 8,000 raises that only to 10: the same 11 examples, seen again. What can go wrong: a rare case the teacher handles perfectly can still vanish in the student, because the teacher was rarely asked it.

steps.title: Why one average hid it.
steps.text: A random sample holds each kind of enquiry in roughly the share it has in real traffic. With 11 under-18s in 8,000, a sample of 200 is expected to hold 200 × 11 ÷ 8,000 = 0.275 of one, so usually none; 2,000 holds about 2.75. The check found 187 of 200 in agreement, 93.5%, and every one of those 200 was an ordinary kind. Even in the 2,000 check, the student refused 1 of 3 under-18s, and two wrong answers barely moved 93.5%. What can go wrong: one average across all kinds lets a kind that is always wrong hide inside a good number. In a5e01's words, a golden set needs a slice for each kind.

steps.title: Small task-specific models: measure per kind.
steps.text: A small model trained for one job, here booking chats, can be much cheaper and quicker: $0.001 and 0.4 seconds a chat against $0.02 and 2 seconds, 20 times cheaper and 5 times faster. That is often worth having. The check before switching works in steps. First, list the kinds of request and score the student on each one, apart. Second, write a must-pass set of the rare cases that must never go wrong, here 40 under-18 requests, kept out of training, and require all of them. Third, if a kind fails, write more examples of it, have the teacher answer them, add them to training and retrain. Fourth, score again before switching. Here 120 added examples took the student from 9 to 40 of 40 at the same price. What can go wrong: a must-pass set only covers what someone thought to write, so keep the hard rules in the system too, like the age question on the form.

steps.title: Not routing, not a new model choice.
steps.text: a2e08 sent easy questions to a cheaper model and kept the hard ones for a stronger one, choosing per question. Distillation is different: the student replaces the teacher for one job, and everything it knows about that job came from the teacher's answers. A router can send a rare question up; a student cannot know that a question is rare unless it was shown such questions in training.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row: the teacher's 8,000 saved answers; 160 under-18 requests written on purpose; 40 of them kept apart as the must-refuse set; 120 answered by the teacher and added to training. Bottom row: the student retrained on 8,120 examples; scored per kind of enquiry; the must-refuse set passed 40 of 40; switched on, with the booking form now asking the age.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: 160 under-18 requests are written on purpose, 40 are kept apart as the must-refuse set, and the teacher answers the other 120, which join the 8,000 saved answers. Bottom row: the student is retrained, scored one kind at a time, and switched on only when it refuses all 40 it has never seen. The booking form asks the age as well.

fix.title: The fix: score the student per kind, with a must-refuse set it must pass in full, and teach it the rare kind before switching
fix.text: List the kinds of enquiry and score the student against the teacher on each one, apart, not on one average. Write a must-refuse set of under-18 requests in the words people really use, keep it out of training, and require 40 of 40 before switching. When it fails, write more such requests, have the teacher answer them, add them to the training examples and retrain; here 120 took it from 9 to 40 of 40 at the same $0.001 a chat. Then check that the other kinds still score as before, 187 of 200. And put the rule somewhere a model cannot forget it: the booking form now asks the age.

limits: A must-refuse set covers only what someone thought to write. A request phrased in a way nobody tried can still slip through, which is why the age question on the form matters.
Scoring per kind needs enough of each kind to mean something. Designs had 25 in the sample of 200; a kind with 2 or 3 tells you very little either way.
Writing 160 requests and retraining took the parlour a weekend. Every new rare rule needs the same work before the student can be trusted with it.

explain.seniorTake: Distillation is a good trade when one job runs at volume: a small student trained on a large teacher's answers can be twenty times cheaper and five times faster. But the student learns only from the examples, never from the teacher's prompt, so every rule in that prompt reaches it only as answers that happened to follow it, and a rule the teacher used 11 times in 8,000 is barely taught at all. Measure a small task-specific model per kind of request, never on one average, because a random sample holds rare kinds at their real, tiny share: 0.275 expected in 200. Write the cases that must never go wrong as a set, keep it out of training, and require all of it before switching. When the student fails it, teach it with more examples of that kind, answered by the teacher, and test again. And keep the hardest rules where no model can forget them: in the form, the code or a person's hands.

realWorld.title: Hinton et al., 2015: a small model for deployment
realWorld.text: Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues start from a cost problem: making predictions using a whole ensemble of models is cumbersome and may be too computationally expensive. Their answer is to compress the knowledge in an ensemble into a single model.

realWorld.title: Hinton et al., 2015: what distillation is for
realWorld.text: In the paper's introduction, the training they call distillation is a way to transfer the knowledge from the cumbersome model to a small model that is more suitable for deployment. The parlour's set-up has its roots in that idea, though the paper's own method trains the small model on the large model's whole spread of likely answers, not just its final reply.

realWorld.title: Amazon Bedrock: teacher and student
realWorld.text: Amazon's user guide defines it in the same words as this case: Model distillation is the process of transferring knowledge from a larger more intelligent model (known as teacher) to a smaller, faster, cost-efficient model (known as student). It adds that the student model's performance improves for a specific use case, which is the catch: one use case, as shown in the examples.

realWorld.title: Amazon Bedrock: training on saved answers
realWorld.text: The guide says you can use existing teacher responses from invocation logs stored in Amazon S3 as training data, which is what Ms Sciarra did with the large model's saved answers. Whatever those saved answers hold, rare cases included, is all the student will see.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023: verification and validation
realWorld.text: A third-party guide to the standard's Annex A lists control A.6.2.4, AI System Verification and Validation, and summarises it as asking organisations to establish robust verification and validation measures for AI systems. That summary is the guide's wording, not the standard's; if you work to the standard, check the control in your own copy.

asked: How would you evaluate a distilled model before switching to it?
When is a small task-specific model the right choice?
interview.answer: A distilled model is a small student trained on a large teacher's answers, so I evaluate it as a copy that may have missed things. First I list the kinds of request it will see and score it against the teacher on each kind apart, because one average over a random sample is mostly the common kinds. I work out the expected count of each rare kind in my sample; if it's below one, the sample hasn't tested it. Then I write a must-pass set of the cases that must never go wrong, especially anything a rule in the teacher's prompt handled, keep it out of training and require it in full. If the student fails, I add more examples of that kind, answered by the teacher, retrain and test again. I'd still keep hard rules outside the model, in the form or the code. A small task-specific model is the right choice for one narrow, high-volume job where cost and speed matter, here twenty times cheaper and five times faster, and where I can name the kinds of request and test each. It's the wrong choice when the job is broad or the rare cases are where the risk lives and I can't write them down. If the company works to ISO/IEC 42001 or reports against SOC 2, that test and the switch are worth recording.

atWork: Look for a cheap model trained on an expensive one's answers and signed off on a random sample. It is a common pattern: a team distils a large model into a small one for one job, checks that they agree on a few hundred random requests, and switches. The first sign of trouble is usually a rare request the large model always handled, now answered wrongly, often one that a rule in the old prompt covered. Ask four things before any switch. What are the kinds of request, and what does the small model score on each one, apart? Which rare cases must never go wrong, and is there a written set of them, kept out of training, that it must pass in full? Did those cases appear in the training examples often enough to learn? And is the hard rule also enforced somewhere outside the model? Build Night: the Nightwatch copilot's X6 compares a small model with an API model on cost and accuracy; score that comparison per kind of request, with a must-pass set, rather than on one average. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 42001:2023 or working toward it, Annex A control A.6.2.4 (AI system verification and validation, as summarised by third-party guides; check the clause on your own copy) is likely to expect a test like the per-kind score and must-pass set to be planned and recorded before release. If you report against SOC 2, criterion CC8.1 covers controlled changes, and swapping the model behind a live assistant is a change to approve, test and record. Building the per-kind test and the must-pass set into the switch now costs far less than explaining a missing one to an auditor later.

recall.prompt: Your team trained a small model on a large model's answers to 50,000 support chats, to cut cost. It matches the large model on 96% of 500 random chats. Policy says it must always hand refund requests over $1,000 to a person, and those show up about once in 5,000 chats. How would you evaluate it before switching?

keyIdeas.idea: The rare case barely appears in a random sample (about 0.1 expected in 500), so the 96% says nothing about it
Score per kind of request, not one average
Write a must-pass set of the rare case, keep it out of training, require it in full; add such examples to training if it fails

recall.model: The 96% is an average over ordinary chats. At about one in 5,000, the big refunds barely appear in a random 500: the expected count is 0.1, so almost none were tested. I'd score the small model per kind of request, refunds, delivery, accounts and so on, and look at each one apart rather than one average. Then I'd write a must-pass set on purpose, say 40 large refund requests in the words customers use, keep it out of training, and require it to pass in full. If it fails, I'd add more examples of that kind, answered by the large model, retrain and score again before switching.

recall.prompt: 11 of the parlour's 8,000 training enquiries came from under-18s. How many under-18 enquiries would you expect in a random sample of 200?
recall.why: Sample size × share: 200 × 11 ÷ 8,000 = 0.275, so most samples of 200 hold none. 2.75 is what a sample of 2,000 would hold; 11 is the whole training set's count.

recall.prompt: A product lead asks when a small task-specific model, trained on a large model's answers, is the right choice, and what it costs you beyond the training run.

keyIdeas.idea: Right for one narrow, high-volume job where cost and speed matter
It learns only what the large model's answers showed; rare cases and rules in the prompt may not come through
So it needs a per-kind evaluation and must-pass set before switching, and hard rules kept outside the model

recall.model: It's the right choice for one narrow, high-volume job, like booking chats or sorting tickets, where it can be twenty times cheaper and several times faster than the large model. The cost is that it only learns what the large model's answers showed it: rules that lived in the prompt, and rare cases the large model was rarely asked, may not come through. So I'd budget for an evaluation per kind of request and a must-pass set of the rare cases before switching, and I'd keep hard rules outside the model as well.

recall.prompt: The teacher costs $0.02 and 2 seconds a chat; the student costs $0.001 and 0.4 seconds. Sending every chat back to the teacher multiplies the cost and the wait by how much?
options: 20 times the cost, 5 times the wait
5 times the cost, 20 times the wait
2 times the cost, 4 times the wait
200 times the cost, 50 times the wait
recall.why: $0.02 ÷ $0.001 = 20, and 2 ÷ 0.4 = 5. At 120 chats a day that is $2.40 a day instead of $0.12.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The retrained student has run since Tuesday 6 October and the form asks the age; nobody under 18 has been booked. Now Ms Sciarra wants a second student for aftercare chats, trained on the teacher's answers to 6,000 aftercare enquiries. I read the teacher's answers: in 4 of the 6,000 the customer described signs of an infection, and each time the teacher told them to see a doctor that day.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What should Ms Sciarra check before switching aftercare to the new student?

keyIdeas.idea: 4 in 6,000 is too few to learn; a random check would expect almost none of them
Write a must-pass set of infection descriptions, kept out of training, that it must pass in full, and add more such examples to training
Score per kind, and keep a hard rule outside the model, such as a person reading any chat that mentions those signs

coldCase.model: The same trap as the under-18 rule. 4 in 6,000 is too few to learn from, and a random check of 200 would expect almost none of them. Before switching, I'd write a must-pass set on purpose, about 40 descriptions of infection signs in customers' own words, keep it out of training, and require it in full. If the student fails, add more such examples, answered by the teacher, and retrain. I'd score every other aftercare question per kind as well. And because this one matters most, I'd keep a rule outside the model: any chat that mentions those signs goes to a person who reads it.
